paragraphs: Friend, here's what I love about this prayer. Solomon just built the most beautiful house anyone had ever seen, and the first thing he says about it is, "The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built." (1 Kings 8:27) The man built a temple and then said it's too small for God. That's humility, and I'm still working on it, because I once stamped one decent cookie and walked around like I invented dough.

So if God is too big for any building, why does the temple matter? Because Solomon asks God to hear, again and again, "from heaven, Your dwelling place." (1 Kings 8:30) The temple is where people turn toward God, and God is the One who listens. Whether it's a defeat, no rain, a plague or a long way from home, Solomon pictures people turning to God, confessing and praying, and he asks God to hear and forgive. He even says plainly, "there is no one who does not sin." (1 Kings 8:46) That means every one of us needs a God who forgives, and this prayer says He is the kind of God people can return to.

And look who else is invited in. Solomon prays for the foreigner who comes from a distant land and asks God to "do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You," so that "all the peoples of the earth will know Your name." (1 Kings 8:43) God's heart was never meant to stay inside one nation's walls. So, baker, whatever you're carrying today, big or small, you can turn toward Him and pray. He hears, and He knows your heart, because "You alone know the hearts of all men." (1 Kings 8:39)
